title: The text discusses the complexities of the Ethiopian revolution, highlighting its initial foreignness to the local populace and the paradoxical outcomes it produced. It notes that while the revolution aimed to modernize and benefit the peasant majority, it often led to new forms of inequality and exploitation, particularly in the context of land reform. The narrative also touches on the rise of the Derg, the military regime that followed, and its brutal repression of dissent, as well as the emergence of separatist movements in various regions. The text reflects on the historical irony of the revolution, where the new leadership inherited the oppressive structures of the past, leading to a cycle of violence and disillusionment among the populace.
